transcript.content: Hi, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?

Yeah, hi. I guess... well, mostly I just don't feel like myself anymore. It's like I'm a completely different person now, or just... empty, I guess. I used to be so active, you know? I mean, I completely stopped hiking. I used to know all the trails around here, had all the right boots and gear, would go out for miles on my days off to clear my head. And I was coaching, too, setting up drills, organizing the schedules, all of that. But I just stopped going. 

Same with my guitar. I've played for years, used to pick it up every single night to decompress after work, but now I don't even look at it. It just sits there in the corner. I don't even call people back anymore. My phone will buzz, and I see who it is, and I just let it ring. I can't bring myself to talk to anyone. I'm staying in this small rental right now, and honestly, some days I just sit there in a chair for hours. Just... sitting. I'll look around and I know exactly what I need to do. I know there are things to do, bills or laundry or whatever, and my brain registers it, but I just can't make myself start. I'll sit there from the morning all the way into the late afternoon and just... not do any of it. I can't get the engine to turn over, if that makes sense.
Did these changes start after something stressful happened in your life?

Stressful... yeah. I mean, you could definitely say that. It was the divorce. My ex-wife and I, we split up, and... well, it's a whole massive process, you know how it is. The paperwork, the arguments, the dividing up of a whole life. I had to leave the house we had together, the one with the garage where I kept all my gear, and that's when I ended up in this rental I was just telling you about. It’s so much smaller. I moved in there about... well, it's been about a year and two months ago now. Fourteen months. 

And that's really when things just started completely unraveling. I remember packing up my boxes, putting my guitar in its case, loading up all my coaching stuff, and just dragging it into this cramped little space. I thought I'd just unpack and get back to my routine, you know, get back on shift and keep my head down. But instead, I just... I put the boxes down and everything just stopped. The stress of the divorce was heavy, sure, but moving into that place... it's been a year and two months of just watching the dust settle on those same boxes. So yeah, fourteen months of just coming apart at the seams ever since I handed over the house keys and walked into that rental. I just haven't been the same since that day.
Have you felt this down or uninterested in things nearly every day for the past two years?

Two years? No, no, not two years. Like I was just saying, it’s been exactly fourteen months. A year and two months. Because two years ago... well, two years ago I was still in the house. I was still married, still doing my regular patrols, pulling my weight on the shift roster, taking the overtime when we were short-staffed. I was completely fine back then. I mean, as fine as anyone is when their marriage is starting to get rocky, right? But I was still getting out there. I was still hiking, still playing my guitar. 

So, no, it hasn't been two years. It started exactly when I moved into that cramped little rental. But since that day? Yeah. Yeah, since that day, it's been every single day. Every. Single. Day. For fourteen months. I wake up, and the sun comes through these cheap plastic blinds the landlord put up—they're always getting tangled, you know the kind, the ones that snap if you pull the cord wrong—and I just look at the ceiling and think... I just can't do it. The whole day just stretches out in front of me like this massive, empty highway that I have to drive down, and I just don't have the gas for it. I'll sit in that chair and watch the light move across the floor from the morning until it gets dark, and I just feel completely hollowed out. And it’s been exactly like that yesterday, the day before, all the way back to when I dropped those boxes on the floor fourteen months ago. So not two years, but for the last four hundred and twenty-something days, yes. Every day.
During these past 14 months, have you felt sad or depressed most of the day nearly every day?

Sad? No. No, I wouldn't say sad. I know what sad feels like, you know? In my line of work—I've been doing protective services, working patrols and security for over twenty years—you see sad things. You see people at the absolute worst moments of their lives. I've had to stand there while people get news that makes them completely collapse on their front porch. I've felt that heaviness in my chest, that real, genuine sorrow. When my dad passed away a few years back, I was sad. I cried. I felt it. 

But this... these last fourteen months? It’s not sadness. Sadness is an emotion. Sadness means you're still feeling something, that your engine is still running even if it's running rough. What I have is just... nothing. It's a total blank. If I was sad about the divorce or losing the house, maybe I'd be looking at old photos, or maybe I'd pull my guitar out of the case and play some slow blues, maybe have a good cry about it. But I don't do any of that. I don't want to do any of that. I just sit in that chair I told you about, the one by the window with those cheap plastic blinds, and I don't feel a single thing. 

It’s like someone went into my brain and just flipped the main breaker switch. Everything just went dark and quiet. There are no tears, no feeling sorry for myself, no heavy grieving. Just a flat, empty void that stretches out all day. I'll watch the clock on the microwave go from 9:00 AM to 4:00 PM, just watching the green numbers change, and my heart rate doesn't go up, I don't get teary-eyed... I just exist. Like a piece of furniture in that room. So, no, I really wouldn't call it feeling sad or depressed. It's more like I've just been completely hollowed out, and there's just no emotion left inside to actually feel sad with.
In the past 14 months, was there ever a period of at least two weeks when you felt down or depressed most of the day?

Doc, I feel like we're kind of going in circles here. Like I was just trying to explain, there hasn't been a two-week period of feeling down, because I haven't felt down at all. Not for two weeks, not for two days, not even for two hours. You're asking if there was a specific window where I got really depressed, like a dip or a valley, right? But my life doesn't have valleys anymore. It's just a flatline. 

Take last December, for example. That's a solid two, three weeks right there around the holidays. Christmas, New Year's... you know, the time when guys in my situation, divorced guys living in a crappy little rental, are supposed to get really down in the dumps. The guys from my shift were texting me, saying things like, 'Hey man, don't get down, come over, have a beer with us.' They figured I’d be sitting in the dark crying into a glass of whiskey because it was my first Christmas out of the house. But I didn't feel down. I didn't feel a thing. 

I just sat in that same chair and watched the snow pile up on the balcony railing outside my window—this ugly, rusted metal railing the landlord refuses to scrape and paint, the paint is just peeling off in these big orange flakes—and I just watched the snow get higher and higher on it. Day after day. I didn't even turn the TV on for the football games. I wasn't depressed about missing Christmas, I didn't feel sorry for myself... I just didn't care that it was Christmas. So, no. No two-week period of being sad or depressed. Just one continuous, unbroken block of fourteen months where the engine is just completely turned off.
During these past 14 months, have you felt hopeless?

Hopeless? No, I wouldn't use that word either. Hopeless implies that you were hoping for something in the first place, right? Like, you have this expectation that things are going to get better, or you're waiting for some big change, and then you realize it's not coming, so you lose hope. You feel hopeless. But I don't have any expectations anymore. I'm not waiting for anything to change. 

I remember back when I first started on the force, you'd see these guys, these older guys who had been on patrol for thirty years, and they were hopeless. They'd sit in the break room, drinking this terrible, burnt coffee from that old percolator we used to have—the one with the cracked glass knob on top—and they'd just complain. They'd talk about how the city was going down the tubes, how the new recruits were soft, how management was screwing them over on their pensions. They were angry and bitter because they had hoped for a good career, a good retirement, and they felt like it was all slipping away. They were hopeless. 

But me? I don't have any of that. I'm not sitting in my apartment, staring at those cheap plastic blinds, wishing my wife would call and say she made a mistake. I'm not hoping the landlord is suddenly going to decide to fix the peeling paint on the balcony railing. I'm not hoping I'll wake up tomorrow and suddenly want to play my guitar again or go for a hike up in the foothills like I used to. I just don't care one way or the other. 

It's like... if you're standing at a bus stop, and you really need to get somewhere, and the bus never comes, you might feel hopeless. But if you're just standing on the sidewalk, and you don't have anywhere to be, and you don't even care if a bus ever drives down that street again... you're not hopeless. You're just standing there. That's me. I'm just standing there. For fourteen months. So, no, doc, I wouldn't say I feel hopeless. I just don't feel anything at all.
Before these last 14 months, was there ever another time in your life when you lost interest in almost everything for at least two weeks?

No, no, I don't think so. Before this... this whole fourteen-month stretch we keep talking about? No. I mean, my life wasn't a parade every day, right? You work in security, you work patrols, you do the graveyard shifts, you get tired. You get burned out. Sometimes you just want to come home, throw your boots in the corner, and sleep for a day and a half. But that's just being exhausted, you know? That's just your body saying it's had enough of the concrete floors and the fluorescent lights and the noise. 

But losing interest in everything? Like I am now? No, never. Before this started, I always had things I cared about. Even when work was rough, or when things with the ex-wife were starting to get tense before the divorce... I still had my stuff. I had my guitar. I've got this old Fender Stratocaster, sunburst finish, beautiful instrument. I used to spend hours just cleaning the frets, restringing it, dialing in the tone on my amp. I loved that. I'd sit out on the back patio of the house—when I still had the house, obviously—and just play for hours. And I used to love hiking up in the foothills, taking the trails up past the reservoir. I had this whole routine on my days off. 

I never went two weeks without wanting to do those things. Even if I was stressed, or if I had a bad week, I'd still look forward to the weekend so I could plug in the guitar or get my boots muddy on the trail. That spark was always there. It might have flickered a bit if I was pulling too many double shifts, but it never just... went out. Not like this. This thing I've got going on now, this total blankness where I don't even want to look at the guitar case... this is completely new. It started fourteen months ago, and before that, I was just a regular guy who liked his hobbies. So, no, nothing like this ever happened before.
Because of this loss of interest and emptiness, have you had trouble doing your job?

Trouble doing my job? Well, yeah, you could say that. Actually, I don't even go in anymore because they suspended me. 

It happened a while back during a routine patrol. I was working the afternoon shift at the main municipal building—you know, the one downtown with the big glass atrium and the revolving doors that always get stuck in the winter? I was doing my regular floor sweep, checking the employee badges, making sure the stairwell doors were secure, just the standard route I've done a thousand times. And I guess... I don't even really know what it looked like from the outside, honestly. I just sort of stopped in the middle of the main lobby. I was just standing there by the directory board, not moving, just completely blanked out, feeling that heavy nothingness we were just talking about. 

But apparently, I was standing there for a really long time, and I guess my face or my posture or something... it really scared the administrative staff. A couple of the receptionists got spooked, and some bystanders who were coming in to the building, they started complaining, saying the protective service guy was acting menacing and staring right through them. Next thing I know, my shift supervisor—this guy Mike who always chews on those little plastic coffee stirrers—he pulls me off the floor. Takes my radio, takes my keys, and tells me I'm suspended because I'm a liability and I'm terrifying the public. 

And the thing is, doc, I didn't even argue with him. I didn't try
Have you had thoughts that life isn’t worth living, or thoughts of killing yourself?

No, no, nothing like that. I mean, I know why you're asking, right? Because I just sat here and told you I don't care about anything, that I'm just standing on the sidewalk watching the bus not come, and that I got suspended from my job because I was just staring at a directory board like a zombie. It sounds bad, I get it. It sounds like a guy who's at the end of his rope. But that's the thing... you have to have a rope to be at the end of it, you know? 

Killing myself? Thinking life isn't worth living? That would take a level of... of energy, or passion, or despair that I just don't have. It's like I was saying before about being hopeless. To want to kill yourself, you have to be in pain. You have to be hurting so bad that you just want the hurting to stop. You have to be sitting in your apartment, looking at those cheap plastic blinds, and crying, or screaming, or feeling like your chest is being crushed in a vice. You have to be feeling *something* so intensely that you'd do anything to escape it. 

I'm not escaping anything. I'm just... existing. It's like my brain has been unplugged from the wall. There's no spark, no power, no nothing. I wake up, I sit on the edge of the bed—it's this old mattress, dips in the middle, I really should have replaced it years ago but I never got around to it—and I just sit there. I don't think, "Oh God, another terrible day, I can't take it anymore." I just think... well, I don't think anything. I just wait until I have to use the bathroom, or until I get thirsty enough to walk to the kitchen for a glass of water. 

There's this guy I knew, back when I was first starting out in security, worked at a mall out in the suburbs. He was going through a really bad divorce, his wife took the kids, took the house, the whole nine yards. He was devastated. You could see it on him, like he was carrying a hundred-pound weight on his shoulders. He used to talk about how he didn't see the point anymore, how he just wanted it all to be over. He was in agony. That's what wanting to die looks like. He was actively wishing for an end to the pain. 

But me? I don't have any pain to end. I don't have any joy, either. It's just a flat line. A big, empty room with nothing in it. And you don't burn down an empty room just because it's empty, right? You just leave it alone. So, no, doc. I haven't had any thoughts about killing myself or that life isn't worth living. I'm not even really thinking about life or death at all. I'm just... here.
During these past 14 months, have you had a marked loss of appetite or lost weight without trying?

Loss of appetite? Or losing weight? No, no, I haven't had anything like that. My weight has stayed exactly the same. I actually have this old mechanical scale in my bathroom—not one of those new digital ones that syncs to your phone or whatever, just the classic dial with the little red line—and I step on it every now and then just out of habit. The needle always hovers right around 195. Hasn't moved an inch in the last year and a half. 

And as for my appetite... I mean, I wouldn't say I've lost it, because I still eat all my regular meals. I don't skip them. It's just that eating has become completely mechanical now, kind of like everything else we've been talking about. I don't get excited about food anymore. I used to love grilling, you know? Back when I had the house, I'd go to the butcher on a Saturday, get a nice thick ribeye, let it sit out to get to room temperature, fire up the charcoal... it was a whole process. I loved the smell of it, the taste of it. Now? Now I just eat because my stomach growls and it's time to put something in it. 

It's like putting gas in a car that's just sitting in the driveway. I'll open a can of soup—usually just the store-brand chicken noodle, nothing fancy—and heat it up on the stove. Half the time I don't even wait for it to get fully hot, I just eat it lukewarm right out of the pot standing in the kitchen because it really doesn't matter to me either way. It all basically tastes like wet cardboard anyway. But the point is, I'm eating the whole can. I'm getting the calories in. Breakfast is usually just two pieces of dry white toast. Dinner is whatever's easy. So I'm definitely eating enough to maintain myself. The uniform pants they made me turn in when they suspended me were a size 36 waist, and if I had to put them on right now, they'd fit exactly the same as they did fourteen months ago. So no, no weight loss, and I'm still eating. It's just a chore now, not something I actually enjoy.
During these past 14 months, have you been sleeping much less or much more than usual?

Sleeping? No, no, my sleep schedule hasn't really changed at all. I'm not sleeping the day away or anything, and I'm not staying up all night either. It's exactly the same as it's always been. 

I usually lay down right around eleven o'clock. I have this old digital alarm clock on my nightstand—one of those vintage Sony Dream Machines with the red LED numbers that are just way too bright, you know the ones? I think I've had it since I got my bachelor's degree. I actually have to drape a t-shirt over it at night so the red glare doesn't light up the whole room. Anyway, I get into bed at eleven, on that same saggy mattress I was telling you about, and I just close my eyes. And I always wake up right around seven in the morning. 

It's like my body is just hardwired for that specific eight-hour block, probably from all those years working the standard morning rotations before they bumped me to the afternoon shift downtown. You'd think a guy who just got suspended, a guy who literally has nowhere to be and nothing to do, would just pull the covers over his head and sleep until noon, right? But I don't. I don't sleep any extra. Seven o'clock rolls around, my eyes open, and I just look up at the ceiling. 

And on the flip side, I'm not tossing and turning with insomnia, either. I'm not pacing the floors at three in the morning. I just get my eight hours, like clockwork, every single night. It's just another mechanical part of the day, just like eating that lukewarm soup. So, no, I haven't been sleeping any more or any less. The actual hours I spend unconscious are exactly the same as they were fourteen months ago. It's just that now, the waking hours in between the sleep feel exactly the same as when I'm asleep. Just... blank. But the sleep itself? No, that hasn't changed a bit.
During these past 14 months, have other people told you that you seem slowed down in how you move or talk?

Other people? No, nobody has said anything like that to me. But, I mean, you have to consider the context here, doc. Who exactly is going to tell me that? It's not like I'm hosting dinner parties or going out to a bar on a Friday night. Since they took my radio and suspended me from the site, I don't really interact with anyone. I live alone. 

The only people I even see on a regular basis are... well, honestly, there's nobody on a regular basis. If I go to the grocery store—I usually go to the big one down on Route 9 because they put in those self-checkout kiosks a few years back—I don't even have to talk to a cashier. I prefer it that way. I just scan my cans of soup and my dry toast, bag it all up, pay the machine, and walk out. I don't have to say a single word about the weather or how my day is going. And my neighbor, Mr. Henderson, he's this older guy who's always out in his driveway fussing with his lawnmower or sweeping up leaves. He used to always try and chat me up when I was walking to my car in my uniform, asking me about the security detail downtown. Now, if he sees me taking the trash out, he just gives me this little nod, and I give him a nod back. That's the absolute extent of my socializing right now. 

So, for someone to tell me I'm talking slower, or moving slower... they'd actually have to be around me enough to have a conversation and notice a difference, right? And nobody is. You're probably the first person I've spoken this many words to in over a year. 

But even just from my own perspective, I don't feel like I'm moving in slow motion or anything. I'm not dragging my feet like I'm walking through wet cement. When I get off that saggy mattress to walk to the kitchen for a glass of water, I just walk to the kitchen. It's the exact same pace I've always walked. I just don't have anywhere important to walk *to* anymore. I'm not rushing to catch a bus or hurrying to clock in for a shift. There's no urgency. But no, nobody has told me I seem slowed down. I'm just existing at my normal speed, just with nowhere to go.
Right now, are you able to manage basic daily self-care, like showering and changing your clothes?

Self-care? Yeah, yeah, I can still do all that. I mean, I'm not... I'm not letting myself go, if that's what you're asking. I still shower every single morning. Right after I wake up at seven, after I lay there looking at the ceiling for a few minutes like I mentioned, I get up and go straight to the bathroom. 

I actually have this showerhead I installed myself a few years ago—one of those low-flow, water-saving ones because the utility bill at this place was just getting completely ridiculous. So I turn it on, and I have to let it run for exactly two minutes so the pipes can warm up. It's an older building, you know, so if you step in right away, it's just ice cold. But I wait the two minutes, I get in, and I use the same brand of Irish Spring bar soap I've been using since I was getting my bachelor's. I don't even bother with shampoo or anything fancy anymore, I just use the bar soap for everything, scrub down, rinse off, and step out. The whole thing takes maybe six or seven minutes. 

And then changing my clothes... yeah, I put clean clothes on. Obviously, I'm not putting on a suit and tie, and I'm definitely not putting on my old security uniform—like I said, I had to turn those in to the supervisor when they suspended me. So my wardrobe these days is pretty basic. It's usually just a pair of gray cotton sweatpants and a plain white t-shirt. I buy those Hanes multi-packs, you know the ones with the reinforced collars so they don't stretch out in the wash? I keep a whole stack of them folded in the second drawer of my dresser. I just pull that drawer open, grab a fresh one, put it on with the sweatpants, and that's my outfit for the day. 

I even still do my laundry every Sunday morning. There's a coin laundromat about two blocks down from my apartment, right next to this old dry cleaner that closed down a while back. I take my plastic basket down there, use the heavy-duty front-loading machines, fold everything right there on those long metal tables they have, and carry it all back. So, yeah, I'm clean. My clothes are clean. I
During these past 14 months, have you had trouble concentrating, like following a TV show, reading, or making simple decisions?

Concentrating? No, I wouldn't say that. My focus is actually... it's just fine. Better than fine, really. I don't have any trouble following things. Take TV, for instance. I don't have the premium cable packages anymore—I cancelled all that when the suspension came down because, you know, I had to tighten up the budget—but I have one of those flat digital antennas hooked up to my television in the living room. It picks up all the local broadcast networks and those weird digital sub-channels they have now. 

There's this one channel that just plays old detective shows all afternoon, back-to-back episodes of *Law & Order* and *Columbo*. I can sit there on the couch and follow the plot perfectly from start to finish. I track all the evidence, I listen to the witness testimonies, I even catch the little continuity errors the directors make, like when a detective is holding a coffee cup in his left hand in one shot and then his right hand in the very next frame. You really can't notice things like that if your concentration is shot, right? I can usually figure out exactly how they're going to break the suspect's alibi by the second commercial break. 

And reading, it's the exact same thing. I don't read a ton of thick novels
During these past 14 months, have you felt worthless?

Worthless? No, I wouldn't use that word. I don't feel worthless. I mean, I know my situation right now isn't exactly... ideal. Being suspended from the site, sitting in my apartment all day in my Hanes t-shirts, not having the radio to listen to the dispatch calls anymore. It's frustrating, absolutely. It feels like I've been sidelined, like I was put on the bench right when I was starting to figure out some of the deeper security protocols they were implementing downtown. 

But worthless implies that I have no value, or that I don't serve a purpose, and I know that's not true. I still have my bachelor's degree, which I worked incredibly hard for. I still have all the training and the observational skills I developed over the years on the job. Just because they took my uniform and told me to stay home doesn't erase what's in my head, you know? I'm still the same person who knows how to secure a perimeter and spot anomalies in a crowd. 

I might not be actively utilizing those skills on a payroll right this second, but that doesn't mean the skills themselves are worthless, and it certainly doesn't mean I am. I'm just... I'm in a holding pattern. Like an airplane circling the airport waiting for clearance to land. The plane isn't worthless just because it's not on the tarmac, right? It's just waiting. That's how I look at it. I'm just waiting for this suspension nonsense to get cleared up so I can get back to doing what I do best. So no, I don't sit around feeling worthless or like I don't matter. I just feel like I'm on pause.
During these past 14 months, have you yourself felt slowed down in your movements, speech, or thinking?

Slowed down? No, no, I haven't felt slowed down at all. If anything, my mind is moving just as fast as it always has, maybe even faster. I mean, thinking-wise, I'm constantly analyzing everything around me. Even when I'm just sitting in my apartment, like I said, watching those old detective shows or looking out the window, my brain is firing on all cylinders. I'm tracking the people walking by on the sidewalk, noting what kind of cars are parked on the street, checking if the streetlights are flickering in any kind of pattern. You have to stay sharp, you know? You can't let your guard down just because you're off the clock. 

And my movements, no, they're perfectly normal. I walk at my usual pace. When I go down to the laundromat on Sundays, I'm not dragging my feet or shuffling along like an old man. I have a very deliberate stride. It's a purposeful walk. In security, you learn how to walk with authority, even when you don't have the uniform on. You keep your shoulders back, your head on a swivel, scanning the environment. I still do that. I can get from my front door to the laundromat in exactly four minutes and thirty seconds if I hit the crosswalk right at Elm Street. I've timed it. 

As for my speech, well, you can hear me right now. I'm not slurring my words, I'm not taking long pauses to figure out what I want to say. I know exactly what I want to say, and I say it. I've always been a clear communicator. When you're calling in a report to dispatch, you have to be concise, you have to enunciate, you have to make sure every single detail is transmitted clearly over the radio because if there's static or interference, they might miss a crucial piece of information. I carry that over into my everyday life. So no, I haven't noticed any slowing down in my thinking, my walking, my talking... none of it. I'm completely up to speed.
Because of these symptoms, are you unable to work at all right now?

Well, it's not that I'm unable to work. Like I was saying before about being in a holding pattern, my skills are completely intact. I am fully capable of working. But... I am not currently working, no. I got suspended from my protective service job. 

And the whole thing was completely overblown, if you ask me. Let me explain exactly how that went down, because it's important context. I was just doing a routine patrol through the main concourse—Section 4, right near the west entrance. I was executing my perimeter checks exactly how we were trained, observing the crowd dynamics, looking for anything out of place. But apparently, my methods... well, management pulled me into the office and told me I had scared some of the retail staff and a few of the bystanders. They said I was being too intense, asking too many questions about who was watching the exits and checking people's bags. I was just trying to secure the area, making sure everything was locked down, but they didn't see it that way. They took my badge, took my radio, and put me on this indefinite suspension. 

And since that happened... I don't know, it just threw my whole schedule off track. It's not just the job that stopped. I used to be really involved in a lot of things outside of work. I was coaching a youth basketball league on Thursday nights down at the community rec center—the 10-to-12-year-old bracket. I had this whole defensive playbook mapped out for the kids, taught them how to watch the opponent's hips to predict their movements. And I used to volunteer on Saturday mornings helping sort out the logistics at the local food pantry. 

But after the suspension came down... I just stopped going. I pulled away from all of it. The coaching, the volunteering... I haven't been back to the rec center in months. I haven't answered calls from the other coaches or the pantry coordinator. I've basically just pulled away from most of the people who used to count on me. It's just... it's easier to stay in the apartment right now. I don't want to have to explain the suspension to everybody, and honestly, I need to be here, keeping an eye on things from my window, staying sharp until this whole misunderstanding at work gets resolved and they put me back on the roster. So yeah, I'm not working, but it's not because I can't. It's just how things have played out.
Have you been hearing or seeing things that other people don’t seem to hear or see?

Well, it's... you know, it's interesting you bring that up. As far as what other people hear or see, I live alone, so I don't have a second set of eyes to verify my observations right now. But I have been logging some highly unusual activity at the apartment. You know they took my work radio, I told you about that. But I have a personal scanner at home. It just keeps me in the loop with local emergency frequencies, helps me stay sharp. The thing is, lately, I've been getting transmissions even when the unit is completely powered down. I mean the volume knob is clicked all the way off, sometimes I even pull the battery pack just to isolate the variable and make sure there's no residual power. But
When you hear those transmissions, are they happening only during the times you feel that empty loss of interest, or do they also happen when your mood feels normal?

Well, it's... it's not like they only happen when I'm feeling that sort of... that empty feeling, you know, the loss of interest in everything. It's not tied to that. I mean, they happen regardless of how I'm feeling. Even on days when I wake up and I feel completely normal, like I'm ready to get back on the job, I'll still get those transmissions. 

Like last Tuesday, for example. I woke up, had my coffee—black, two sugars, just like always—and I felt fine. I felt sharp. I was reviewing some old incident reports I kept from my training days, just brushing up on protocol, and I felt completely engaged. My mood was perfectly normal. And right in the middle of reading a report on crowd control tactics, I heard it. Clear as day.
